```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

```{r setup}
library(nlmixr2est)
```

A *likelihood penalty* is an extra term added to the objective function while a
model is estimated.  Examples are a ridge (L2) penalty on network weights that an
`rxode2` model extension adds to the model, a smoothness penalty, or a
subject-level prior that the model block cannot express.

`nlmixr2est` gives compiled code one C interface for these terms.  Every
estimation method then honors it.  This vignette is for **package developers**
who write such an extension.

## Three kinds of terms

| Term | Called | Scale | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| per observation | once per observation, inside the subject loop | log-likelihood | read `d(LL)/d(f)`, add a per-observation term |
| per subject | once per subject (and per ETA trial) | log-likelihood | eta priors, subject-level regularization |
| population | once per objective evaluation | `-2LL` (objective) | ridge/lasso on thetas, network weight penalties |

The per-observation hook is the older contribution registry
(`inst/include/nlmixr2estLikContrib.h`).  It is described in
`vignette("extending-nlmixr2est")`.  This vignette covers the per-subject and
population terms in `inst/include/nlmixr2estLikPenalty.h`.

The scales differ on purpose:

* A subject term adds log-likelihood. A constant `c` on each of `N` subjects
  therefore moves the objective by `-2 * N * c`.
* A population term returns a penalty `P` on the objective scale, so it moves
  the objective by `P`.

## The C interface

```c
#include <nlmixr2estLikPenalty.h>

typedef struct {
  int nsel; const int *sel;       // thetas named in the spec (0-based)
  int npar; const double *par;    // numeric settings from the spec
  void *data;                     // opaque pointer from the spec / bundle
} nlmixrPenCtx;

typedef struct {
  int id, neta, nobs, ntheta;
  const double *eta, *theta;      // current etas; natural-scale thetas
  double *llik;                   // += extra log-likelihood
  double *dLL_deta;               // [neta] += d(LL)/d(eta), may be NULL
} nlmixrPenSubj;

typedef struct {
  int ntheta, neta, nsub;
  const double *theta, *omega;    // natural thetas; current omega (may be NULL)
  double *dObj_dtheta;            // [ntheta] += gradient, NULL when not wanted
} nlmixrPenPop;

typedef struct {
  int abi;                        // NLMIXR_PEN_ABI
  int flags;                      // NLMIXR_PEN_IN_OBJF, NLMIXR_PEN_NO_GRAD
  const char *name;
  void   (*subject)(nlmixrPenSubj *s, const nlmixrPenCtx *ctx);     // optional
  double (*population)(nlmixrPenPop *p, const nlmixrPenCtx *ctx);  // optional
  void *data;
} nlmixrLikPenalty;
```

Thetas are always the **natural-scale** model thetas in the order of the
`ui$iniDf` theta numbers (`ntheta`), including fixed thetas.  The
estimator-specific scaling and parameter maps are handled for you.

### Rules for the callbacks

* `subject` runs **inside the OpenMP subject loop**.  It must not call the R API
  or allocate memory.  Any per-subject state must be keyed by `id`.  Allocate
  buffers from R, on the main thread, before the fit.  `id` is the 0-based
  subject index; mixture components of the nonparametric methods use ids beyond
  the subject count.
* `population` runs on the main thread, once per objective evaluation.
* Fill `dLL_deta` whenever the subject term depends on the etas.  FOCEi-type inner
  problems use it to find the conditional mode.
* Fill `dObj_dtheta` when it is non-NULL, or set `NLMIXR_PEN_NO_GRAD`.  The
  methods then fall back to finite differences.  Only the population gradient is
  used analytically.  There is no omega gradient slot: when the term reads
  `omega`, its omega derivative is taken by finite differences.
* `omega` is the current between-subject covariance in `ini()` eta order.
  Every method with random effects passes it, and its omega update (the EM and
  variational M-steps included) minimizes the penalized objective; emvi, fbvi
  and vae penalize only the variances, not the covariances, and saem leaves the
  variances of mixture-split and pooled (IOV) etas unpenalized.  The
  population-only methods (the nlm family) pass `neta = 0`.  A subject term that writes a non-zero value switches the
  FOCEi analytic outer gradient (`fast = TRUE`) to finite differences, because
  it moves the conditional mode.

## A worked extension

The C side of a small package `myPen` defines an L1-like (smoothed) penalty on
the selected thetas and a subject-level shrinkage on the etas:

```c
#include <R.h>
#include <Rinternals.h>
#include <math.h>
#include <nlmixr2estLikContribPtr.h>   // also brings in nlmixr2estLikPenalty.h

iniNlmixr2estLikContribGlobals

// population: lambda * sum(sqrt(theta^2 + eps)), -2LL scale
static double myPop(nlmixrPenPop *p, const nlmixrPenCtx *ctx) {
  double lambda = ctx->npar > 0 ? ctx->par[0] : 0.0, eps = 1e-6, ret = 0.0;
  for (int j = 0; j < ctx->nsel; ++j) {
    int t = ctx->sel[j];
    double a = sqrt(p->theta[t] * p->theta[t] + eps);
    ret += lambda * a;
    if (p->dObj_dtheta != NULL) p->dObj_dtheta[t] += lambda * p->theta[t] / a;
  }
  return ret;
}

// subject: LL -= 0.5 * kappa * sum(eta^2)
static void mySubj(nlmixrPenSubj *s, const nlmixrPenCtx *ctx) {
  double kappa = ctx->npar > 1 ? ctx->par[1] : 0.0;
  for (int q = 0; q < s->neta; ++q) {
    *s->llik -= 0.5 * kappa * s->eta[q] * s->eta[q];
    if (s->dLL_deta != NULL) s->dLL_deta[q] -= kappa * s->eta[q];
  }
}

static const nlmixrLikPenalty myPenalty = {
  NLMIXR_PEN_ABI, 0, "myPen", mySubj, myPop, NULL};

SEXP _myPen_iniPtrs(SEXP p) { return iniNlmixr2estLikContrib(p); }

SEXP _myPen_ptr(void) {
  return R_MakeExternalPtr((void *) &myPenalty, R_NilValue, R_NilValue);
}
```

Add `LinkingTo: nlmixr2est` to the `DESCRIPTION`.

The R side refreshes the pointer table on load.  It is only needed if the
package also registers session-wide or per-observation bundles:

```r
.onLoad <- function(libname, pkgname) {
  .Call(`_myPen_iniPtrs`, nlmixr2est::.nlmixr2estLikContribPtrs())
}
```

### Attaching the penalty to a model

A model extension owns the model, so it attaches the penalty to the model.  The
penalty is then active only while that model is estimated:

```r
myPenSpec <- function(thetas, lambda = 1, kappa = 0) {
  nlmixr2est::nlmixr2LikPenaltySpec(
    ptr = function() .Call(`_myPen_ptr`),  # resolved when the fit starts
    thetas = thetas, par = c(lambda, kappa), inObjf = FALSE
  )
}

# for example from the extension's rxode2 UI handler
ui <- nlmixr2est::nlmixr2LikPenaltyAdd(ui, myPenSpec(c("w1", "w2"), lambda = 0.1))
```

Pass `ptr` as a function rather than an external pointer.  Pointers do not
survive `saveRDS()`, but the function is called again each time a fit starts.

A user can supply the same specs for a single call instead:

```r
fit <- nlmixr2(model, data, "focei", likPenalty = list(myPenSpec("tka", 10)))
```

## A model term that brings its own penalty

The most useful form of an extension is a function the user writes inside
`model({})`.  The function creates its own parameters and registers its own
penalty, so the user never sees either step.  The `nlmixr2spline` package is a
complete, tested example of this: `spline(WT)` adds a penalized B-spline
(P-spline) of a covariate.

```r
library(nlmixr2spline)
one.cmt <- function() {
  ini({
    tka <- 0.45; tcl <- 1; tv <- 3.45
    eta.ka ~ 0.6; eta.cl ~ 0.3; eta.v ~ 0.1
    add.sd <- 0.7
  })
  model({
    ka <- exp(tka + eta.ka)
    cl <- exp(tcl + spline(WT, k = 6, lambda = 10) + eta.cl)
    v <- exp(tv + eta.v)
    linCmt() ~ add(add.sd)
  })
}
fit <- nlmixr2(one.cmt, nlmixr2data::theo_sd, "focei")
fit$likPenalty   # the spline's roughness penalty at the estimates
```

Three pieces make this work.

### 1. Expand the term in two stages

rxode2 calls an `rxUdfUi` S3 method for every call it does not know.  The
method returns the code that replaces the call (`replace`), extra lines
(`before`/`after`) and an updated `iniDf` holding any new parameters.  A
spline needs the data to place its knots, but a model is parsed before the
data exist.  So the term expands in two stages:

```r
rxUdfUi.spline <- function(fun) {
  # validate the arguments, then defer to a placeholder with fixed arity
  list(replace = "rxSplineData(WT, 6, 10, 2, 3, 0, 0)", uiUseData = TRUE)
}
attr(rxUdfUi.spline, "nargs") <- NULL           # spline() takes named arguments

rxUdfUi.rxSplineData <- function(fun) {
  data <- rxode2::rxUdfUiData()
  if (is.null(data)) return(list(replace = fun, uiUseData = TRUE))
  # ... knots from the data, new thetas in iniDf, the penalty (below) ...
  list(replace = "(spline.WT.1*(rxSplineB(WT, 54.6, 86.4, 6, 3, 2) - 0.175) + ...)",
       iniDf = newIniDf)
}
attr(rxUdfUi.rxSplineData, "nargs") <- 7L      # the placeholder's arity
```

`uiUseData = TRUE` marks the model as needing its data.  `nlmixr2()` then
re-parses the model with the estimation data available through
`rxode2::rxUdfUiData()`, and `rxSolve()` does the same with its event table.
The placeholder (`rxSplineData()`) keeps the user's settings in the model
text, so the data-free model stays valid rxode2 code.

### 2. Hide the algebra, not the parameters

nlmixr2nn keeps its network opaque: the model text holds a single compiled
call, `nn<K>(id, x)`.  Its weights are not nlmixr2 parameters at all.  They sit
in hidden covariate slots, and nlmixr2nn trains them in its own loop.  That
works for nlmixr2nn because nlmixr2est never estimates the weights.  It does
not work for a term whose parameters nlmixr2est *should* estimate.
rxode2 builds every sensitivity (the FOCEi inner problem, the analytic outer
gradient, the nlm-family gradients) symbolically from the model text, so a
parameter read behind its back has a derivative of zero.

The spline therefore hides the *basis* and keeps the coefficients as
ordinary thetas:

* `rxSplineB(x, lo, hi, k, degree, j)` is a C function registered with rxode2
  (`R_RegisterCCallable()` plus a row in `rxode2parseAssignTranslation()`).
  Its x-derivative is registered with `rxode2::rxD()`, so rxode2 can
  differentiate through it.
* Each coefficient multiplies one basis call.  The term is linear in its
  thetas, so every theta derivative is exact and needs nothing special.
* All the knot information is in the call's arguments.  Nothing has to be
  rebuilt after `saveRDS()`, and there are no parameter offsets that differ
  between estimators.
* rxode2 looks model functions up by name when it builds derivatives, so the
  package also exports R versions of `rxSplineB()`/`rxSplineBd()`.  For that
  reason the package must be attached (`library(nlmixr2spline)`).

### 3. Register the penalty while expanding

The expansion knows the new theta names and the penalty matrix, but an
`rxUdfUi` method can only return code and an `iniDf`.  The method calls
`nlmixr2LikPenaltyUdf()` instead:

```r
nlmixr2est::nlmixr2LikPenaltyUdf(nlmixr2est::nlmixr2LikPenaltySpec(
  ptr = .splinePenaltyPtr,                 # function returning the C bundle
  thetas = c("spline.WT.1", "spline.WT.2", "spline.WT.3", "spline.WT.4", "spline.WT.5"),
  par = c(lambda, as.vector(S)),           # lambda, then the penalty matrix
  inObjf = FALSE,
  name = "spline(WT)"                      # unique per term; reused names replace
))
```

`nlmixr2()` collects the specs registered during its data re-parse and
attaches them to the expanded model with `nlmixr2LikPenaltyAdd()`.  They then
behave exactly like any other per-model penalty: active only for this fit,
saved with the fit's model, and reported in `fit$likPenalty`.  Outside of an
`nlmixr2()` expansion (for example in `rxSolve()`) the call does nothing.

The C side is a population penalty on the selected thetas, here
`lambda * b' S b` with its gradient:

```c
static double splinePop(nlmixrPenPop *p, const nlmixrPenCtx *ctx) {
  int n = ctx->nsel;
  if (ctx->npar != 1 + n * n || p->theta == NULL) return 0.0;
  double lambda = ctx->par[0], ret = 0.0;
  const double *S = ctx->par + 1;
  for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
    double si = 0.0;
    for (int j = 0; j < n; ++j) si += S[i + j * n] * p->theta[ctx->sel[j]];
    ret += p->theta[ctx->sel[i]] * si;
    if (p->dObj_dtheta != NULL) p->dObj_dtheta[ctx->sel[i]] += 2.0 * lambda * si;
  }
  return lambda * ret;
}
```

A spline's coefficients have no random effect, so each estimator treats them
as plain population parameters.  The FOCEi family and the nlm family estimate
them well.  `saem` also applies the penalty, but it estimates thetas without a
random effect with a short derivative-free search inside a stochastic
approximation, and that converges slowly for a many-coefficient spline.

## Built-in penalties

Two built-in penalties are useful for testing and teaching:

* `"thetaL2"`: `par[1] * sum((theta - par[2])^2) + par[3]` on the selected thetas.
* `"etaL2"`: `par[2] - par[1]/2 * sum(eta^2)` added to each subject's
  log-likelihood.

```{r}
ridge <- nlmixr2LikPenaltySpec("thetaL2", thetas = "tka", par = 10)
ridge
```

```{r, eval = FALSE}
one.cmt <- function() {
  ini({
    tka <- 0.45; tcl <- 1; tv <- 3.45
    eta.ka ~ 0.6; eta.cl ~ 0.3; eta.v ~ 0.1
    add.sd <- 0.7
  })
  model({
    ka <- exp(tka + eta.ka)
    cl <- exp(tcl + eta.cl)
    v <- exp(tv + eta.v)
    linCmt() ~ add(add.sd)
  })
}
fit <- nlmixr2(one.cmt, nlmixr2data::theo_sd, "focei",
               likPenalty = list(ridge))
fit$likPenalty    # value of each penalty at the estimates
```

## Is the penalty part of the objective?

By default a penalty only shapes the estimation.  The reported `OBJF`, `AIC`,
`BIC` and log-likelihood are those of the penalized estimates **without** the
penalty, so a penalized model stays comparable with an unpenalized one.  Set
`inObjf = TRUE`, or `NLMIXR_PEN_IN_OBJF` in the bundle's `flags`, to report the
penalized objective instead.  Either way, `fit$likPenalty` lists each penalty's
population value, summed subject log-likelihood and objective contribution.

Objective types added after the fit, for example with `setOfv()`, are computed
without the penalties.

## Method coverage

Every method is tagged with `attr(nlmixr2Est.<est>, "nlmixr2LikPenalty")`:

| Methods | Subject term | Population term |
|---|---|---|
| focei, foce, fo, foi, focep, laplace, agq (with their `i`/`m`/`f` variants), posthoc | inner problem, conditional mode and objective | objective and (analytic) outer gradient |
| imp, impmap, qrpem | E-step through the FOCEi inner likelihood | M-step of the mu-referenced thetas and objective |
| saem | MCMC acceptance and the quadrature objective | M-step (penalized Newton refinement of the mu-referenced thetas), the direct optimization of thetas without a random effect, and objective |
| vae, emvi, fbvi | ELBO data term | penalized M-step (vae intercepts, emvi thetas), prior on the population draw (fbvi), and objective |
| nlm, nlminb, optim, bobyqa, newuoa, uobyqa, n1qn1, lbfgsb3c, trust | once per subject, no etas | objective and gradient |
| npag, npb | conditional density of every support point | mu-referenced theta update; added to the reported objective after the fit (a warning says so) |
| nlme, nls | not supported: the fit stops | |
| simulation / prediction | ignored | |

The nlm family includes external drivers.  `nlmObjectiveSetup()`, `nlmSolveR()`
and the `nlmixr2NlmEval()` C API evaluate the same objective, so an external
optimizer or sampler driving them sees the penalty too.

A mu-referenced family (`mfocei` and the other `m*` methods) solves for its
mu-referenced thetas in closed form.  A population penalty on such a theta
therefore makes the outer gradient fall back to finite differences.  The
penalty enters the objective, but the closed-form step itself does not see it.
Covariate effects added by the `vae` covariate selection are not penalized.

### Adding support to a new method

A method written in another package opts in with

```r
attr(nlmixr2Est.myMethod, "nlmixr2LikPenalty") <- "full"   # or "subject"
```

Its objective must then include the active penalties.  A method built on the
FOCEi inner problem (`likInner0`) or on the nlm objective gets both terms
automatically.

## Session-wide registration

`nlmixrRegisterLikPenalty()` and `nlmixrRemoveLikPenalty()` (pointer table
entries 6 and 7 of `.nlmixr2estLikContribPtrs()`) register a bundle for every
fit in the session.  The bundle's `data` and `flags` are used as given.  Prefer
per-model specs.  If you do register globally, unregister in `.onUnload()`:
`nlmixr2est` keeps the raw function pointer and cannot tell that your DLL has
gone away.
